title: Tensor-Network Finite Elements for Analytic Operator Equations
authors: Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk, Michael J. Landry, Chu-Liang Fu, Mingda Li
abstract: Operator equations (OEs) underpin quantitative modeling across science and engineering. Finite-element (FE) methods discretize continuous OEs into finite-dimensional algebraic systems, whereas tensor networks (TNs) provide flexible variational representations of correlated discrete systems. Here, we develop a framework that connects FE with TN for analytic OEs. The power of this method comes from its ability to convert highly non-linear partial differential equations into linear matrix equations. In particular, we show that FE discretization induces a hierarchy of multilinear interaction tensors, through which differential, integral, nonlinear, memory, and delay equations can be expressed within a common algebraic structure. The resulting systems are reformulated as weighted-residual optimization problems over TN degrees of freedom. Matrix-product-state calculations for one-dimensional linear and nonlinear diffusion reproduce conventional solutions with controlled error while preserving continuity and Neumann boundary conditions. The framework provides a common variational language for analytic OEs and establishes a direct connection between FE numerical formalism and TN variational algorithms, offering a general foundation for TN-based and quantum-inspired approaches to solving OEs.
summary: The paper introduces Tensor-Network Finite Elements, a novel framework that unifies the solution of diverse operator equations—from PDEs to delay equations. It achieves this by translating continuous differential operators into structured tensor forms and minimizing the resulting residual error within a constrained TN variational space. This offers a general, powerful computational tool for modeling complex physical systems.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a unified framework to solve analytic Operator Equations (OEs), including PDEs, IDEs, and MDEs, by connecting Finite-Element (FE) discretization with Tensor Network (TN) variational representations.
main_result: The authors establish a direct connection between the FE numerical formalism and TN variational algorithms, allowing highly non-linear partial differential equations to be reformulated as weighted-residual optimization problems over TN degrees of freedom.
method: The method involves discretizing OEs using FE methods, which generates multilinear interaction tensors. These are then approximated and optimized within a Tensor Network ansatz (like MPS or PEPS) by minimizing a weighted residual norm subject to the TN manifold constraint.
model_or_system: The framework is general, applying to various OEs such as nonlinear diffusion equations, initial-value problems, integro-differential equations, and memory/delay equations. The underlying mathematical structure involves mapping continuous operators onto discrete tensor representations.
key_observables: Controlled error reproduction of conventional solutions (e.g., 1D diffusion), preservation of boundary conditions (Neumann).
important_parameters: Bond dimensions ($\sigma$), maximum bond degree ($M$), time step size ($\Delta t$), and the order of basis expansion ($B$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions include assuming locality of correlation to use MPS/PEPS ansatzes, and that the solution admits a compact tensor-network representation for computational tractability.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the contraction of interaction kernels in TNs. Figure 2 shows the TN representation of an operator's left-hand side. Figures 7 and 8 demonstrate numerical convergence tests on nonlinear diffusion problems using both standard methods and the proposed TN variational approach.
paper_structure: The paper builds from general FE discretization theory to handling non-linearity by upgrading the Hilbert space to Fock space. It then shows how the resulting large coefficient tensors are compressed via TN ansatzes, culminating in optimization procedures tested on specific diffusion examples.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful computational bridge between established numerical analysis (FEM) and modern quantum many-body simulation techniques (TNs), offering a general toolset for solving complex physical models beyond standard quantum chemistry or condensed matter simulations.
